wine.name: Tom Cullity Cabernet Sauvignon Malbec
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority, with Malbec for most of the rest; a little Petit Verdot joined some of the early vintages.
wine.sites: The Home Vineyard at Wilyabrup: the founder's blocks of 1967, old Houghton clone Cabernet on its original roots, with later plantings around them, dry grown in old gravel loam beside the Wilyabrup Brook.
wine.making: Whole berries, picked by hand, begin a wild fermentation and are pumped over several times a day. The wine is then aged for about eighteen months in French oak barriques, the larger part of them new, before bottling.
wine.glass: Blackberry, cassis and ripe plum over liquorice, dark chocolate and a smoky, savoury note of nori; full yet poised, with fine, firm tannin and fresh acidity.
wine.ageing: Closed and firm for its first five years or so, it opens over the following decade and is made to keep for twenty years and more when the year is strong.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour or two, an old one gently off its sediment; a Bordeaux glass.

label.means: The founder's name, given to the house's leading red from the 2013 vintage.
Australian law lists the grapes of a blend in descending order, so Cabernet is the larger share.
The Geographical Indication: at least 85 per cent of the fruit must come from it.

records.table: Tom Cullity, the leading red of Vasse Felix, carries the name of the doctor who planted the region's first modern commercial vineyard there in 1967. Cabernet Sauvignon with Malbec from his Home Vineyard, it is dark and firm, with a long finish; give it air.
records.story: Climate research of the mid 1960s likened the cape to Bordeaux, and Dr Tom Cullity (1925 to 2008), a Perth heart specialist, took it up and went looking for land. In 1967 he planted a small vineyard at Wilyabrup, the first modern commercial vineyard of Margaret River, with Cabernet Sauvignon and Malbec among the first vines, and called it Vasse Felix. In 1972 he made a Cabernet Sauvignon Malbec and a Riesling, which the house counts as the region's first serious wines. Cullity sold the estate in the mid 1980s, and in 1987 a Perth family bought it. For years the house's leading red was the Heytesbury, a Cabernet led blend. To mark fifty years since the first planting, the house released in 2017 the 2013 vintage of a new flagship, named for the founder and grown in the Home Vineyard around his old vines, with Malbec in the blend as it had been in 1972. Tom Cullity took the Heytesbury red's place at the head of the range. One bottle holds the region's beginning: the first modern vineyard, the first grapes and the man who planted them, poured as a wine for the cellar.

others.name: Heytesbury
others.note: The Cabernet led blend that headed the house's reds until Tom Cullity took its place; the name then went to the Chardonnay alone.

others.name: Heytesbury Chardonnay

traps: Tom Cullity is Cabernet Sauvignon with Malbec, not a straight Cabernet; Malbec has been in the house's red since its first of 1972.
The vines date from 1967 but the wine does not: the first Tom Cullity is the 2013 vintage, released in 2017.
Vasse Felix is in Margaret River in Western Australia, a long way from every South Australian region.

questions.exp: Malbec has partnered Cabernet in the house's red since 1972 and gives the second name on the label; Merlot, the usual partner in Bordeaux, plays no part.

questions.exp: Cullity planted in 1967, the region's first modern commercial vineyard; 1971 is when the Cullens planted their vineyard nearby, and 1972 the year of his first wines.

report: The founder's dates rest on the house's own history pages (1925 to 2008, a cardiologist), with his birth on 10 September 1925 confirmed by the State Library of South Australia; two further searches found no obituary or second source for the year of death, so 2008 stands on the house's page alone and the refuter may wish to try a newspaper archive.

The making rests on the importer Winebow's sheets of 2019 and 2021, a sheet of 2022 and The Real Review: wild yeast, whole berries, about eighteen months in French barriques with a new share from about half to four fifths by vintage, so the record says the larger part.

The first vintage of 2013 released in 2017, and Tom Cullity taking the Heytesbury red's place, rest on Decanter and The Buyer; the house's own story page has the founder hand the estate on in 1984 (to a couple, living or not, left unnamed) and another account gives a sale of 1985, so the story says the mid 1980s; the Holmes à Court purchase of 1987 rests on the house's page and a second profile.

Wikipedia says the first harvest of 1971 was lost to birds and bunch rot, and a mirror of it explains the name as a lucky or happy Vasse; neither found a second source, so both are left out, and say is empty for want of a source on how the house says its name.

The library's Heytesbury line calls it the long standing Cabernet blend of the house; Decanter and The Buyer say Tom Cullity supplanted the Heytesbury red from the 2013 vintage, so the record tells it as the earlier leading red.
The Wikipedia entry and one profile place the first vineyard at Cowaramup; the house gives the Home Vineyard's locality as Wilyabrup, which the record follows.

The first commercial vineyard of the region rests on the house's pages and Wikipedia; that the founder acted on the climate research of the mid 1960s rests on the library and the region record, not on a source read here, and the refuter may wish to try it.
Farmed organically was cut from sites: the house's organic farming is recent and not a habit of decades.

wine.name: Moss Wood Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority, with small amounts of Cabernet Franc and Petit Verdot.
wine.sites: The Moss Wood vineyard at Wilyabrup, first planted in 1969: old, dry grown, low yielding vines.
wine.making: Fermented in small open fermenters, the cap of skins plunged by hand several times a day. Each batch then rests apart in French oak barriques, a quarter or fewer of them new, for well over a year and a half before the blend is made, and the blend often goes back to barrel, so the wine has more than two years in oak in all.
wine.glass: Blackcurrant, plum and cherry over cedar, tobacco and bay leaf; medium to full in body, with bright acidity and fine, supple tannin, generous without losing its frame.
wine.ageing: Approachable young but built to keep: a strong vintage holds its freshness for decades, as the 1975 has shown.
wine.serve: Pour at 16 to 18 degrees Celsius into a Bordeaux glass, decanting a young bottle for an hour or so and an old one gently off its sediment.

label.means: The name of the vineyard and of the estate, planted at Wilyabrup in 1969.
A grape named alone on an Australian label must be at least 85 per cent of the wine.
A Geographical Indication on the cape in the south west of Western Australia.

records.table: Planted at Wilyabrup in 1969, Moss Wood was the second commercial vineyard of Margaret River, and its Cabernet Sauvignon is the wine of that vineyard. It spends two years and more in French oak and keeps for decades, its blackcurrant, plum and bay leaf set on fine tannin.
records.story: Vasse Felix was two years old when, in 1969, a doctor and his wife bought land at Wilyabrup and planted Cabernet Sauvignon there, the young region's second commercial vineyard. The first wine came with the 1973 vintage, and the 1975 Cabernet became the house's measure: the winemaker later told Decanter it was the first international recognition of the cape's Cabernet. In 1979 the founders took on a winemaker and viticulturist, and in 1984 he and his wife leased the estate; by July 1985, as the house tells it, the sale was complete. The new owners later added the neighbouring Ribbon Vale vineyard and kept its wines under their own label, so Moss Wood Cabernet stays the wine of the vineyard of 1969. The house is patient with it: the Cabernet's batches are blended late and the wine has more than two years in barrel; tasted at twenty seven years old, the 1975 showed fine acidity and freshness. Margaret River Cabernet, it shows, can be generous and yet keep its shape for decades.

others.name: Moss Wood Ribbon Vale
others.note: Wines of a neighbouring Wilyabrup vineyard the house added later, kept under their own label.

others.name: Moss Wood Sémillon
others.note: Margaret River Sémillon, riper and fuller than the Hunter's.

traps: Moss Wood was planted in 1969, two years after Vasse Felix: it is the region's second commercial vineyard, not its first.
Margaret River Sémillon such as Moss Wood's is riper and often fuller than the low alcohol Hunter Valley style.

questions.exp: The house gives the wine more than two years in French barriques, only a small share of them new, rather than American casks, old vats or a short spell in steel.

questions.exp: The 1975 is the vintage the house and Decanter single out; 1973 was the first vintage, 1969 the year of planting and 1985 the year of the sale.

One profile calls Moss Wood the first winery to plant Cabernet Sauvignon in the region; Vasse Felix planted Cabernet in 1967 by its own account, so the claim is left out.

The library's holdings line (run since the 1980s) fits the sale of 1985, but the winemaker arrived in 1979; the 1973 first vintage made in a tin shed with a milk vat rests on one source and is left out.
The soil of the vineyard is not given: no source read named it, so sites keeps to the slopes and the dry farming.

The new oak share (15 to 20 per cent in the vintages of 2012, 2016, 2019 and 2021) and the late blending, with the blend often returned to barrel for its last months, rest on the house's vintage pages; the first draft's blended only at the end is corrected.

wine.name: Diana Madeline
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority, with small amounts of Merlot, Cabernet Franc and Malbec.
wine.sites: The biodynamic Cullen Vineyard at Wilyabrup: Cabernet Sauvignon planted in 1971, Merlot and Cabernet Franc in 1976 and Malbec in 1978, on old granite and gravelly sandy loam over lateritic subsoil.
wine.making: Picked by hand on fruit days of the biodynamic calendar and fermented with no yeast, acid or malolactic culture added, some lots staying for weeks on their skins. The wine is then aged for some thirteen to fifteen months in barriques and puncheons, about half of them new.
wine.glass: Cassis, mulberry and plum over cedar, graphite and violet, with a note of iodine and ironstone; fine grained, chalky tannin and a long, cool finish.
wine.ageing: Supple enough to enjoy young, it holds for two decades and more, and the house claims as long as half a century for a strong year.
wine.serve: 16 to 18 degrees Celsius in a Bordeaux glass; an hour or two in a decanter for a young bottle, careful decanting off the sediment for an old one.

label.means: Named for the founder Diana Cullen; the wine was once labelled simply Cabernet Sauvignon Merlot.
The family name of the founders, Kevin and Diana Cullen, who planted the vineyard in 1971.
Wilyabrup, where the vineyard lies, is a district of this Geographical Indication, not a registered subregion.

records.table: Biodynamic and picked by the moon, Diana Madeline is the Cabernet blend of Cullen Wines, named for the founder who planted the Wilyabrup vineyard with her husband in 1971. Mostly Cabernet Sauvignon, it is fine, cool and long.
records.story: Before any vines, Dr Kevin Cullen (1922 to 1994), the Busselton doctor who drove the Busselton Health Study, and his wife Diana Cullen (1923 to 2003) farmed land at Wilyabrup. In 1965 they thought of sowing lupins, and the agronomist they asked suggested vines instead. In 1966 they planted a small trial plot; as the family tells it, the young vines were sprayed with weedkiller by mistake while the couple were away, and pulled out. In 1971 they planted again, on their own land, and the Cullen Vineyard grew from there, with Merlot and Cabernet Franc in 1976 and Malbec in 1978. Diana Cullen led the winemaking from 1981, their daughter took it on in 1989, and the vineyard was certified biodynamic in 2004. The Cabernet blend, long labelled Cabernet Sauvignon Merlot, took the name Diana Madeline at the start of the 2000s in honour of its founder, and the Chardonnay became Kevin John, for her husband. This is the cape's Cabernet as it becomes when the farming leads and nothing is added in the cellar.

The society spells her second name Madeleine; the wine is Madeline.
The year the wine took the name Diana Madeline is the 2001 vintage by Decanter and the 2000 vintage by another account, so the record says the start of the 2000s.

Biodynamic certification is 2004 for the vineyard and 2008 for the winery on the house's pages and one importer's; another house page says certified since 2005, so the label line follows the more common reading.

The library's trap calls Wilyabrup a Margaret River subregion; the region record and the register know it only as an unofficial district (Margaret River has no registered subregion), so the record says a district.
Living people kept out: the founders' daughter, who has made the wine since 1989, and the lupin researcher who suggested vines, whose status was not settled.
The making follows the house's sheets of 2020 to 2024: thirteen to fifteen months in oak, forty to fifty five per cent new, barriques and puncheons, no added yeast, acid or malolactic culture.
The label's Biodynamic line was cut: no source read showed that the label prints the word, so the label keeps to the name, the house and the region.

wine.name: Art Series Chardonnay
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone, of the Gingin clone, whose small berries carry slightly more sugar and acidity.
wine.sites: Estate blocks with northern aspects and rows running east to west; Block 20, by the front gate and planted in 1976, is the backbone, with fruit of Block 22 beside it.
wine.making: Hand picked fruit is destemmed cool, given some skin contact, settled and fermented with cultured yeast in new French oak barriques, then aged on its lees, stirred often, for about eleven months. It is bottled after a light fining and released about three years after the vintage.
wine.glass: Grapefruit, lime curd and white nectarine over poached pear, then toasted hazelnut, cashew and a flinty edge; rich and layered, with taut acidity that carries a long finish.
wine.ageing: Tight on release despite its years at the estate; it gains nut and honey over a decade and, in a strong year, keeps well beyond it.
wine.serve: 10 to 13 degrees Celsius, not too cold; decant a young bottle briefly if it seems closed; a wide white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The estate's leading range, each label carrying a work by a contemporary Australian artist.
The region on the label, which must give at least 85 per cent of the fruit; here all of it is estate grown.

records.table: In the early 1970s a Napa vintner judged the Leeuwin Estate property right for fine wine, and its white flagship is the Art Series Chardonnay. Fermented and aged in new French oak and held about three years before release, it pairs grapefruit and cashew with taut acidity.
records.story: In 1972, the year the house gives, or 1973 by another account, the Napa Valley vintner Robert Mondavi (1913 to 2008) visited the property and judged it right for fine wine; he went on to mentor its owners. The estate dates itself to 1973: a nursery went in in 1974, and from 1975 the vineyard blocks were planted by hand. Block 20, by the front gate, went in in 1976. The first commercial vintage was 1979, and in 1980 came the first Art Series Chardonnay, the estate's first wine with a painting on its label, by a Western Australian artist: the start of a long line of labels carrying Australian paintings. Decanter in London singled out one of its first vintages, the 1980 or the 1981 by different accounts. The wine is fermented in new French oak, bottled some eighteen months after the vintage and released about three years after it, so a bottle on a list is older than most whites beside it. Of Margaret River's whites, it is the one a guest is likely to know by name.

others.name: Art Series Cabernet Sauvignon
others.note: The red of the same range, framed like Bordeaux and often overshadowed by the white.

others.name: Art Series Riesling

The Art Series Chardonnay is released about three years after its vintage, so a current release is not a young wine.

wine.name: Cape Mentelle Cabernet Sauvignon
wine.grapes: Cabernet Sauvignon, the great majority, with Petit Verdot and a little Merlot.
wine.sites: Estate vineyards that began with Wallcliffe, planted in 1970 on a ridge of free draining lateritic gravel from decomposed ironstone over gravelly clay; Trinders and other estate vineyards join it by vintage.
wine.making: Each batch is fermented apart, with wild and selected yeasts, and some stay on their skins for weeks after fermentation. The wine is then matured on its fine lees in oak, chiefly French barriques and much of it new, for fourteen to twenty months by vintage before the blend is bottled.
wine.glass: Mulberry, blackcurrant and cassis with a leafy lift of fresh herbs, black olive, nori and liquorice; cocoa, cedar and violet come with age, over fine, sleek tannin.
wine.ageing: Firm and fruited young, it opens after about ten years; a strong vintage, the house says, runs to twenty years and more.
wine.serve: At 16 to 18 degrees Celsius, in a Bordeaux glass; decant a young bottle for an hour or two and an old one slowly, leaving its sediment behind.

label.means: A headland of the cape's coast, named by a French expedition of 1803 for a French geographer.
The cape between Cape Naturaliste and Cape Leeuwin, registered as a Geographical Indication.

records.table: Cape Mentelle Cabernet Sauvignon took the Jimmy Watson Trophy, the Melbourne show's prize for a red a year old, in 1983 and again in 1984. From estate vineyards that began with Wallcliffe in 1970, it brings mulberry, cassis and black olive and a sleek, fine tannin.
records.story: Three brothers founded Cape Mentelle in 1970 and named it for the nearby headland, which a French expedition had named in 1803 after a French geographer of the day. One of them, who had studied winemaking in California, made the wines. They planted the Wallcliffe Vineyard on lateritic gravel, adding Zinfandel in the early 1970s, a grape he had met in California, and the first Cape Mentelle wines came in the mid 1970s. In 1983 the 1982 Cabernet Sauvignon won the Jimmy Watson Trophy at the Royal Melbourne Wine Show, the award for a dry red a year old, and in 1984 the 1983 won it again: two wins in a row for a region whose first modern commercial vines went in only in 1967. The 1983 came from a hot, dry year, and the house says cool ocean breezes spared it the worst of the heat. In 1985 the founding winemaker went on to found Cloudy Bay in Marlborough, New Zealand. Veuve Clicquot took a stake in Cape Mentelle at the start of the 1990s and full ownership in 2000, and in 2023 it returned to Australian hands. The two trophies mark the years the cape's Cabernet won the notice of the whole country.

questions.q: On what soil does the Wallcliffe Vineyard of Cape Mentelle grow its Cabernet Sauvignon?
questions.exp: The house describes free draining lateritic gravel from decomposed ironstone over gravelly clay; terra rossa over limestone is Coonawarra's soil, not Margaret River's.

questions.q: Which vintages of Cape Mentelle Cabernet Sauvignon won the Jimmy Watson Trophy?
questions.exp: The 1982 won in 1983 and the 1983 in 1984, since the trophy is judged on reds a year old; 1970 is the founding year and 2000 the year Veuve Clicquot took full ownership.

report: The house is not in the library: the founding of 1970 by three brothers, the trophies of 1983 and 1984 for the 1982 and 1983 vintages and the Veuve Clicquot purchase rest on the house's history page, Wikipedia and Decanter; the stake is 1990 and a half in two accounts and 1991 and seventy per cent in one, so the story says the start of the 1990s, with full ownership in 2000 in both.

The founding winemaker and his brothers are living or of unsettled status and are not named; his study in California is the house's (Fresno State) and Decanter's, and Cloudy Bay in 1985 is the house's newsletter with Decanter naming him its founder.

Edme Mentelle's dates were cut: the year of his death is 1815 in a Western Australian place name guide and 1816 in Wikidata and DBpedia, so the story describes him as a French geographer of the day; the naming of 1803 by the Baudin expedition rests on Wikipedia and that guide.

The first Cape Mentelle wine is dated 1976 in one house newsletter and 1974 in another, so the story says the mid 1970s; the Zinfandel planting is 1972 in one house source and 1974 in another, so the story says the early 1970s.

The house's own newsletter of 2023 announces its purchase by Paragon, and Decanter reported the sale by Moët Hennessy to an Australian group, so the story closes on the return to Australian hands in 2023 without naming the buyer.

The making and the sites rest on the house's sheets of 2016 and 2018: batches fermented apart, wild and selected yeasts, up to 35 and 65 days on skins, eighteen to twenty months on fine lees, about 55 per cent new oak in 2016 and four fifths in 2018, mostly French; the fruit came from Wallcliffe, Crossroads and Chapman Brook in 2016 and from Trinders and Wallcliffe in 2018, so sites no longer gives Wallcliffe alone.

The house also bottles a Heritage Cabernet Sauvignon from the old Wallcliffe vines alone, and its 2022 Cabernet Sauvignon draws on parcels across its vineyards with fourteen months in oak; the range has changed under its owners, so the checker may wish to confirm which bottling carries the line of the trophy wines.

changed: wine.making: about eighteen months, half or more of the oak new, becomes fourteen to twenty months by vintage, much of it new: the author's own reading of the house's sheets gives eighteen to twenty months with 55 and 80 per cent new for 2016 and 2018 and fourteen months for 2022, and Decanter has the 1983 at twenty months, a third new.
story: a region whose first commercial vines went in only in 1967 becomes first modern commercial vines, in the Margaret River Wine Association's words, as in the Vasse Felix record.
open: The house bottles a Heritage Cabernet Sauvignon from the old Wallcliffe vines beside the estate Cabernet; the record keeps the estate Cabernet, the line of the two trophy wines, and the integrator may wish to watch how the range settles.

The first Cape Mentelle wine is 1976 in one house newsletter and 1974 in another, and the Veuve Clicquot stake is 50 per cent in 1990 by Wikipedia and 70 per cent in 1991 by Decanter; the story keeps the mid 1970s and the start of the 1990s.
